title: Why is the sky blue?
one_liner: Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths of sunlight far more strongly than red ones, so blue light reaches us from every direction of the sky.
summary: Sunlight contains every visible wavelength. As it crosses the atmosphere, nitrogen and oxygen molecules scatter part of it in all directions, and the strength of that Rayleigh scattering rises with the inverse fourth power of wavelength. Blue light near 450 nm is therefore scattered about four times more than red light near 700 nm. We see the scattered light as a blue dome; violet is scattered even more but the solar spectrum, ozone absorption and the eye's sensitivity tip the balance to blue.
analogy: It is like a pinball table where small, fast balls bounce off every pin while big, slow ones roll straight through: blue light is the small ball.
takeaways: Rayleigh scattering by molecules much smaller than the wavelength scales as 1 over wavelength to the fourth power.
Blue is scattered about 4 times more than red, so the diffuse skylight is blue.
The sky is not violet because sunlight has less violet, ozone absorbs some, and our cones respond weakly to it.
Sunsets are red because the long path through air removes most blue before the light reaches us.

sections.heading: Sunlight meets the atmosphere
paragraphs: The Sun emits a broad spectrum that peaks in the green-blue part of the visible range. Before scattering, that mix looks white.
Roughly 99 percent of the atmosphere is nitrogen and oxygen, molecules around a thousand times smaller than visible wavelengths. That size ratio puts them in the Rayleigh regime.
points: White sunlight holds every visible wavelength

sections.heading: Rayleigh scattering
paragraphs: An oscillating electric field induces a dipole in each molecule, which re-radiates light. The radiated power scales with the fourth power of frequency, giving the 1/λ⁴ law.
Larger particles such as water droplets and dust scatter all wavelengths more evenly (Mie scattering), which is why clouds and haze look white or grey.
points: Scattering strength rises steeply as wavelength shrinks

diagram.caption: Molecules and droplets scatter light very differently.

sections.heading: Why not violet?
paragraphs: Violet is scattered even more than blue, yet the sky does not look violet. Sunlight carries less violet, ozone high up absorbs some of it, and our short-wavelength cones respond weakly there.
The visual system combines the scattered spectrum into a hue that matches a sky blue, slightly desaturated by the remaining white light.

diagram.caption: Three factors turn a violet-rich spectrum into a blue sky.

sections.heading: Sunsets and the daily cycle
paragraphs: At sunrise and sunset light crosses up to 40 times more air. Most blue is scattered out of the beam before it arrives, leaving reds and oranges.
The same physics runs every day as the Sun's angle changes the path length.

diagram.caption: Path length through the air sets the colour through the day.

caveats: Pollution and aerosols add Mie scattering and wash the blue toward white.
Exact perceived hue depends on observer, altitude and humidity.
